subtype: Trying fully and accepting the result [Response]
passage: In the village of Thenzawl, Lalremsiami had spent four months on one puan for the district handloom fair: a new pattern of river stones she had designed herself. Other years she had entered old designs at the last minute and said, if she lost, 'I didn't really try.' This year she tried. She rewove the border twice. She asked the oldest weaver in the village to look at it and tell her the truth. On the day, the judges gave the prize to a weaver from Champhai. Lalremsiami's piece got nothing. That evening Yogesh, who ran the stall next to hers, found her writing in a notebook. 'Not upset?' 'Upset,' she said. 'But I know it's my best. The judge said the colours fight in the middle. Now I know what to fix.' She underlined it: colours, middle.

qa.q: How long did Lalremsiami spend on the puan?
qa.a: She spent four months on it.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami feel after getting no prize?
qa.a: She felt upset but steady, because having given her best, the result became useful information instead of a blow she needed to excuse.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami do that turned the loss into growth?
qa.a: She wrote down the judge's point, that the colours fight in the middle, as the specific thing to fix.

qa.q: How might Yogesh see her reaction?
qa.a: Yogesh seems surprised she isn't only upset, and likely respects how calmly she takes the feedback.

grounding: An adult prepares fully for a weaving competition, and when she wins nothing she treats the result as information for growth.

subtype: Trying fully and accepting the result [Response]
passage: For years Anders had joked that he'd try stand-up 'someday, when I'm not so busy'. This spring in Copenhagen he stopped hiding behind busy. He wrote a five-minute set, practised it in the shower, recorded himself, and ran it for Priscila twice at her kitchen table. 'If it bombs,' he told her, 'at least it'll bomb properly.' On open-mic night at the bar, the audience laughed twice: once at the bike joke, once at the sandwich joke. The rest was polite silence. Walking home, Priscila waited for him to say he hadn't really been ready. Instead he said, 'So. Bike and sandwich work. The middle two minutes don't. I know that because I actually did my best.' He sounded tired and a bit bruised, but not ashamed. The next week he signed up again.

qa.q: How many times did the audience laugh?
qa.a: The audience laughed twice, at the bike joke and the sandwich joke.

qa.q: How did Anders feel walking home, and why?
qa.a: He felt tired and a bit bruised but not ashamed, because having truly prepared, the quiet parts were information rather than a verdict to hide from.

qa.q: What did Anders gain from giving full effort?
qa.a: He learnt exactly which jokes worked and which two minutes didn't, so he could rework the set and sign up again.

qa.q: What did Priscila expect Anders to say, and how might she feel instead?
qa.a: She expected an excuse about not being ready, and would likely feel surprised and impressed by his honest review.

grounding: An adult prepares properly for a risky first stand-up set and treats the lukewarm response as information to grow from.

subtype: Playing for its own sake [Actor]
passage: On a quiet Saturday in Addis Ababa, Esther sat on the courtyard steps with a box of chalk. Nobody was watching. Her brother Abebe was inside with his homework. She drew a sun, then a goat, then a long road with little houses. She hummed. She rubbed out a wobbly roof with her palm and drew it again. When the chalk was a tiny stub, she sat back, looked at the road for a moment, and nodded. Then she dusted her hands and went inside to find Abebe, without calling anyone to come and see.

qa.q: What did Esther draw first?
qa.a: She drew a sun first.

qa.q: Why did Esther keep drawing when nobody was watching?
qa.a: She was enjoying it; her humming shows she felt happy and absorbed, and drawing was fun all by itself.

qa.q: What could a parent do to protect this kind of play?
qa.a: Leave her be, keep chalk handy, and not turn her drawing into a contest or offer prizes for it.

qa.q: How might Abebe feel if he came out and saw the road?
qa.a: He might feel surprised and pleased, even though Esther hadn't made it for him.

grounding: A young child draws in chalk for a long time with no audience, simply for fun, and stops when she feels finished.

subtype: Playing for its own sake [Actor]
passage: At the anganwadi, the other children had gone out to the swings, but Bhupen stayed on the corner mat with the wooden blocks. He was building a long, crooked train. He talked softly to himself: 'This one is the engine. This one carries mangoes.' Mehak Didi, the teacher, watched from the doorway and didn't say anything. For almost an hour he added carriages, knocked one over, fixed it, added a bridge. Then he stood up, looked at it, said 'Done', and ran outside. He didn't ask anyone to come and look.

qa.q: What was Bhupen building?
qa.a: He was building a long, crooked train.

qa.q: Why did Bhupen stay inside when the others went to the swings?
qa.a: He was happily absorbed in his train and enjoying the building itself, which is why he talked to himself and didn't need anyone to watch.

qa.q: What did Mehak Didi do well?
qa.a: She watched quietly without interrupting or praising, letting the play stay his own.

qa.q: What would change if Mehak Didi had offered a star for the best train?
qa.a: Bhupen might start building to win the star, and the fun of building just for himself could fade.

grounding: A young child builds with blocks for almost an hour for the pleasure of it and stops when he feels done.

subtype: Playing for its own sake [Actor]
passage:
Monday. After lunch, Eshaan spread newspaper on the balcony floor and painted blue circles, humming. Nobody had asked him to.
Wednesday. He painted again, this time a big red boat. His brother Mohit asked, 'Who's it for?' Eshaan shrugged. 'Nobody. It's for painting.'
Friday. Eshaan painted a green tree with birds for a long, long time. Then he put the brush in the water, looked at the tree, and said, 'Finished.' He left it on the balcony to dry and went to play with his cars.

qa.a: He painted a big red boat.

subtype: Reward replacing interest [Actor]
passage:
School library note, Class 4, end of term.
Before the reading challenge, Divyansh was the child I had to chase out at the bell. He once spent three weeks on a thick book about volcanoes and told me every chapter. Since we started giving a star sticker for each book finished, with a prize at twenty stars, he has read twenty-two books in six weeks. Almost all are the thin picture books from the lower shelf, which he finishes in ten minutes at the counter. When I asked about the volcano series, he said, 'Those take too long. I'd only get one star.' He no longer tells me what the books are about. He asks how many stars he has. Next step: I'll end the star chart after this month, set up a 'tell me one thing you found' corner instead, and talk to his class teacher.
Afreen

qa.q: How many books has Divyansh read in six weeks?
qa.a: He has read twenty-two books in six weeks.

qa.q: Why does Divyansh now choose the thin picture books?
qa.a: He has become eager for stars and the prize, so the thick books he used to love feel like a waste of time, and his interest in what's inside has faded.

qa.q: What change does the librarian plan, and why?
qa.a: Ending the star chart and starting a 'tell me one thing you found' corner, to bring the focus back to the joy of reading rather than counting.

qa.q: What might Afreen feel noticing he only asks about stars?
qa.a: Afreen likely feels disappointed and a little worried, missing the reader who used to tell every chapter about volcanoes.

grounding: A librarian's note shows a child who loved thick books switching to thin ones once a star reward is offered, as the joy of reading fades.

Papa's new rule: one cricket card for every book I finish. I've got nine cards this week! Yogesh only has four. I picked all the short books from the shelf, the ones with big letters. I finished three today before lunch.
The jungle story book Nani gave me is still on my table. I was really liking it, the part with the wolves. But it's so thick, it would take a whole week, and that's only one card. So I put it back in the cupboard.

subtype: Reward replacing interest [Actor]
passage: The small library in the panchayat office at Khandala had one shelf of children's books, and Dhruv had read most of them twice, sitting on the floor with his knees up. In June, the volunteer, Zainab Didi, started a scheme: a peda from the sweet shop for every book returned. Dhruv began taking the thinnest books, the ones with twelve pages, and bringing them back the same afternoon. He collected eleven pedas in a week. One day Zainab Didi held up the fat book about sailors he used to love. 'Don't you want this again?' Dhruv shook his head. 'It's just one peda.' He took two thin books instead and ran off without opening either. Zainab Didi watched him go, then quietly took the peda jar off the counter.

qa.q: What did Zainab Didi give for each book returned?
qa.a: She gave a peda from the sweet shop.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv refuse the book about sailors?
qa.a: He had become eager for pedas, so a long book he once loved felt like a poor trade, and his joy in reading slipped behind the reward.

qa.q: What could Zainab Didi do next?
qa.a: Remove the peda scheme, as she begins to, and invite children to share what they liked in a book instead.

qa.q: What might Zainab Didi feel watching Dhruv run off?
qa.a: She likely feels disappointed and a little regretful that her reward scheme changed how he reads.

grounding: A village child who loved reading starts picking the thinnest books once sweets are offered per book, and the joy fades.

subtype: Studying only for marks [Actor]
passage: With the power out and the board exam mock at eight the next morning, Vijay sat by an emergency lamp and crammed the chemistry chapter, line by line, the way Papa liked. Only what was in last year's paper; nothing else counted. He didn't wonder why sodium burned bright yellow; he just memorised that it did. He scored 49 out of 50, first in the class. Papa smiled and told the neighbours. A week later his younger sister Chandrika came home excited from a science show. 'Why does salt make the flame yellow? You know chemistry!' Vijay opened his mouth. He had written the answer a week ago. Now there was nothing there. 'It's not in the syllabus,' he said, annoyed. Chandrika looked disappointed. 'But isn't it interesting?' Vijay didn't answer. He wasn't sure he had ever found any of it interesting.

qa.q: What did Vijay score in the mock?
qa.a: He scored 49 out of 50, first in the class.

qa.q: Why did Vijay feel annoyed at Chandrika's question?
qa.a: He felt uncomfortable and a little embarrassed that he had forgotten something he wrote a week ago, since he had learnt it only for marks.

qa.q: What could Vijay try to keep what he learns?
qa.a: Ask 'why' while studying, explain topics to Chandrika, and treat the syllabus as a starting point rather than the only thing that counts.

qa.q: How does Chandrika see chemistry?
qa.a: Chandrika finds it exciting and full of questions, and is disappointed that her brother doesn't share that curiosity.

grounding: A teenager crams for rank and his father's approval, scores top marks, and a week later has forgotten the answer and feels no curiosity.

passage: In her room in Tolichowki, Parveen had a chart on the wall: every test, every rank, highlighted in green when Abbu was pleased. She was second in Class 10. qa.a: She was second in Class 10.

grounding: A teenager studies only for rank and her father's approval, cramming what will be tested and forgetting it, while a classmate reads out of curiosity.

subtype: Studying only for marks [Actor]
passage:
'Ninety-four in history!' Nirmala hugged her daughter. 'Rank?'
'Third,' Sangeeta said. 'Revathi got ninety-six.'

qa.q: What could Nirmala change in how she responds to marks?
qa.a: She could ask what Sangeeta found interesting before asking about rank, showing she values learning, not only scores.

qa.q: What does Nirmala realise when she says 'I forgot to want the rest'?
qa.a: She realises her focus on marks and rank may have pushed out her daughter's curiosity, and she feels a pang of regret.

grounding: A teenager who studies only for marks and her mother's approval scores well but remembers nothing, and her mother begins to notice the cost.
